paragraphs.heading: A contest in space
paragraphs.text: The Space Race was a contest between the United States and the Soviet Union, rivals in the Cold War, over who could do more in spaceflight. It grew out of the nuclear arms race between the two after World War II, a race built on ballistic missiles. Doing well in space was seen as vital to national security, especially for long-range missiles and spy satellites. It also became a symbol of each side's culture and beliefs.

paragraphs.heading: Rockets from the war
paragraphs.text: Before the war, Germans, Americans and Soviets had tried small liquid-fuel rockets, but reaching space needed larger ballistic missiles. One such missile was Wernher von Braun's A-4, better known as the V-2, which Nazi Germany built to bomb the Allies. After the war both the US and the USSR took over German rocket assets and used them to speed up their own missiles. In October 1957 the Soviets tested the world's first working intercontinental ballistic missile, or ICBM: a missile able to hit targets on the far side of the globe in a short time. This perceived threat stirred fears in the US that became known as the 'missile gap', and the first American ICBM, Atlas, was tested in late 1958.

paragraphs.heading: Dreams in print and on screen
paragraphs.text: Public interest came first from the Soviet side. In October 1951 rocket engineer Mikhail Tikhonravov wrote "Flight to the Moon" for Pionerskaya pravda, a newspaper for young readers, describing a future two-person spaceship. American magazines soon followed: from 1952 to 1954 Collier's ran seven articles on von Braun's plans for crewed flight. In March 1955 an animated Disneyland episode, "Man in Space", reached about 40 million US viewers and stirred public excitement and government interest in both countries.

paragraphs.heading: Sputnik and Gagarin
paragraphs.text: The race began on 29 July 1955, when the US announced it would launch satellites for the International Geophysical Year. Five days later the Soviet Union said it would launch one too, "in the near future". On 4 October 1957 the USSR put up Sputnik 1, the first successful satellite, setting off the "Sputnik crisis" in the West. On 12 April 1961 Yuri Gagarin became the first human in space, on the orbital flight of Vostok 1. A run of further Soviet firsts followed over the next few years.

paragraphs.heading: The race to the Moon
paragraphs.text: Gagarin's flight pushed President John F. Kennedy to raise the stakes. On 25 May 1961 he asked Congress to commit to landing a man on the Moon and bringing him home safely before the decade was out. Both sides built super heavy-lift rockets, and the American Saturn V was big enough to send a three-person orbiter and a two-person lander to the Moon. Apollo 11 met Kennedy's goal in July 1969, and five more Apollo crews later landed. The Soviet N1 rocket never succeeded, and the USSR eventually dropped its crewed Moon plans to focus on Salyut, the first space station program, and on the first landings on Venus and Mars.

paragraphs.heading: From rivals to partners
paragraphs.text: In April 1972 the two sides agreed on a joint mission, the Apollo–Soyuz Test Project. In July 1975 an American crew and a Soviet crew met in Earth orbit, and the two countries developed a shared docking standard, called APAS-75. Many observers see this as the race's final act, though rivalry gave way to teamwork only slowly. After the Soviet Union collapsed, the US and the new Russian Federation agreed in 1993 on Shuttle–Mir and the International Space Station.
